claim: Adolescence is a stage of fast growth and development.
source: Adolescence is a stage of fast growth and development.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about adolescent development.

claim: Exposures during puberty can have long-term effects on health in later life.
source: Exposures during puberty can have long-term effects on health in later life.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction and represents established scientific consensus.

claim: Exposures during early life have long-term effects on later health.
source: Epidemiological studies of life course have indicated that exposures during early life have long-term effects on later health (Kuh et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kuh et al., 2003.

claim: Unhealthy environments and lifestyle habits during rapid cell division can affect the structure or functions of organs, tissues, or body systems.
source: Unhealthy environments and lifestyle habits during rapid cell division can affect the structure or functions of organs, tissues, or body systems, and these changes can subsequently affect health and disease in later life (Biro and Deardorff, 2013; Power et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Biro and Deardorff, 2013 and Power et al., 2013.

claim: Lower birth weight and fast growth during childhood predispose individuals to coronary heart disease and increased blood pressure in adulthood.
source: For example, lower birth weight and fast growth during childhood predispose individuals to coronary heart disease and increased blood pressure in adulthood (Osmond and Barker, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Osmond and Barker, 2000.

claim: Adolescence is characterized by pubertal maturation and growth spurts.
source: Adolescence is characterized by pubertal maturation and growth spurts.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about adolescent development.

claim: Early pubertal development is linked to worse health conditions, such as obesity and cardiometabolic risk factors in adulthood.
source: Early pubertal development is linked to worse health conditions, such as obesity and cardiometabolic risk factors in adulthood (Prentice and Viner, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Prentice and Viner, 2013.

claim: Childhood obesity can lead to early onset of puberty, especially among girls.
source: However, childhood obesity can lead to early onset of puberty, especially among girls (Li et al., 2017; Richardson et al., 2020), and, therefore, can confound the observed associations between early pubertal development and worse later health.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2017 and Richardson et al., 2020.

claim: Early pubertal development is linked to substance use and other risky behaviors in adolescence.
source: Moreover, early pubertal development is linked to substance use and other risky behaviors in adolescence (Hartman et al., 2017; Savage et al., 2018), but the associations are partly explained by familial factors (Savage et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hartman et al., 2017 and Savage et al., 2018.

claim: The associations between early pubertal development and substance use/risky behaviors are partly explained by familial factors.
source: Moreover, early pubertal development is linked to substance use and other risky behaviors in adolescence (Hartman et al., 2017; Savage et al., 2018), but the associations are partly explained by familial factors (Savage et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Savage et al., 2018.

claim: Many unhealthy lifestyle choices, such as smoking initiation, alcohol use, and a physically inactive lifestyle, are already made in adolescence and increase the risk of developing several noncommunicable diseases over the following decades.
source: Many unhealthy lifestyle choices, such as smoking initiation, alcohol use, and a physically inactive lifestyle, are already made in adolescence and increase the risk of developing several noncommunicable diseases over the following decades (Lopez et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lopez et al., 2006.

claim: Unhealthy habits initiated in adolescence are likely to persist into adulthood.
source: Once initiated, unhealthy habits are likely to persist into adulthood (Latvala et al., 2014; Maggs and Schulenberg, 2005; Rovio et al., 2018; Salin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Latvala et al., 2014; Maggs and Schulenberg, 2005; Rovio et al., 2018; and Salin et al., 2019.

claim: Healthy habits tend to cluster during childhood and adolescence.
source: A recent systematic review showed that healthy habits tend to cluster during childhood and adolescence, and typically, about half of the adolescents fall into subgroups characterized by healthy lifestyle habits (Whitaker et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Whitaker et al., 2021.

claim: About half of adolescents fall into subgroups characterized by healthy lifestyle habits.
source: A recent systematic review showed that healthy habits tend to cluster during childhood and adolescence, and typically, about half of the adolescents fall into subgroups characterized by healthy lifestyle habits (Whitaker et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Whitaker et al., 2021.

claim: Small minorities of adolescents are classified as heavy substance users or as having multiple other risk behaviors.
source: However, small minorities of adolescents are classified as heavy substance users or as having multiple other risk behaviors (Whitaker et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Whitaker et al., 2021.

claim: The long-term consequences of the accumulation of unhealthy adolescent behaviors on health in later life have been rarely studied.
source: The long-term consequences of the accumulation of unhealthy adolescent behaviors on health in later life have been rarely studied.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, representing a knowledge gap.

claim: Epigenetic alterations, including age-related changes in DNA methylation (DNAm), constitute a primary hallmark of biological aging.
source: Epigenetic alterations, including age-related changes in DNA methylation (DNAm), constitute a primary hallmark of biological aging (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to López-Otín et al., 2013.

claim: Epigenetic clocks are algorithms that aim to quantify biological aging using DNAm levels within specific CpG sites.
source: Epigenetic clocks are algorithms that aim to quantify biological aging using DNAm levels within specific CpG sites.
evidence: This is a definition based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The first-generation clocks, Horvath's and Hannum's clocks, were trained to predict chronological age.
source: The first-generation clocks, Horvath's and Hannum's clocks, were trained to predict chronological age (Hannum et al., 2013; Horvath, 2013), whereas the second-generation clocks, such as DNAm PhenoAge and GrimAge, are better predictors of health span and lifespan (Levine et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hannum et al., 2013 and Horvath, 2013.

claim: The second-generation clocks, such as DNAm PhenoAge and GrimAge, are better predictors of health span and lifespan than first-generation clocks.
source: The first-generation clocks, Horvath's and Hannum's clocks, were trained to predict chronological age (Hannum et al., 2013; Horvath, 2013), whereas the second-generation clocks, such as DNAm PhenoAge and GrimAge, are better predictors of health span and lifespan (Levine et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Levine et al., 2018 and Lu et al., 2019.

claim: The DunedinPoAm estimator has been developed to predict the pace of aging.
source: The DunedinPoAm estimator differs from its predecessors in that it has been developed to predict the pace of aging (Belsky et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Belsky et al., 2020.

claim: The pace of aging describes longitudinal changes over 12 years in several biomarkers of organ-system integrity among same-aged individuals.
source: The pace of aging describes longitudinal changes over 12 years in several biomarkers of organ-system integrity among same-aged individuals.
evidence: This is a definition based on the cited literature about DunedinPoAm.

claim: DunedinPACE was trained to predict pace of aging measured over 20-year follow-up.
source: Recently, the DunedinPACE estimator, which constitutes an advance on the original DunedinPoAm, was published (Belsky et al., 2022). DunedinPACE was trained to predict pace of aging measured over 20-year follow-up, and only the reliable probes were used in the prediction.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Belsky et al., 2022.

claim: Several lifestyle-related factors, such as higher body mass index (BMI), smoking, alcohol use, and lower leisure-time physical activity (LTPA), are linked with accelerated biological aging measured using epigenetic clocks.
source: Previous studies have linked several lifestyle-related factors, such as higher body mass index (BMI), smoking, alcohol use, and lower leisure-time physical activity (LTPA), with accelerated biological aging measured using epigenetic clocks (Oblak et al., 2021; Quach et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Oblak et al., 2021 and Quach et al., 2017.

claim: Most studies on lifestyle and biological aging were based on cross-sectional data on older adults.
source: However, most of these studies were based on cross-sectional data on older adults.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of previous studies in the literature.

claim: Advanced pubertal development, higher BMI, and smoking are associated with accelerated biological aging in adolescence.
source: The first studies on the associations of adolescent lifestyle-related exposures with biological aging assessed with epigenetic aging measures indicated that advanced pubertal development, higher BMI, and smoking are associated with accelerated biological aging in adolescence (Etzel et al., 2022; Raffington et al., 2021; Simpkin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Etzel et al., 2022; Raffington et al., 2021; and Simpkin et al., 2017.

claim: The study participants originated from the longitudinal FinnTwin12 study (n = 5114).
source: The study participants originated from the longitudinal FinnTwin12 study (n = 5114).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: Adolescent lifestyle-related factors, including body mass index (BMI), leisure-time physical activity, smoking, and alcohol use, were based on self-reports and measured at ages 12, 14, and 17 years.
source: Adolescent lifestyle-related factors, including body mass index (BMI), leisure-time physical activity, smoking, and alcohol use, were based on self-reports and measured at ages 12, 14, and 17 years.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methods.

claim: Blood-based DNA methylation (DNAm) was used to assess biological aging with six epigenetic aging measures in young adulthood (21–25 years, n = 824).
source: For a subsample, blood-based DNA methylation (DNAm) was used to assess biological aging with six epigenetic aging measures in young adulthood (21–25 years, n = 824).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methods and sample size.

claim: Five subgroups of participants with different adolescent lifestyle behavior patterns were identified.
source: We identified five subgroups of participants with different adolescent lifestyle behavior patterns.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on latent class analysis.

claim: When DNAm GrimAge, DunedinPoAm, and DunedinPACE estimators were used, the class with the unhealthiest lifestyle and the class of participants with high BMI were biologically older than the classes with healthier lifestyle habits.
source: When DNAm GrimAge, DunedinPoAm, and DunedinPACE estimators were used, the class with the unhealthiest lifestyle and the class of participants with high BMI were biologically older than the classes with healthier lifestyle habits.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on the analysis of epigenetic aging measures.

claim: The differences in lifestyle-related factors were maintained into young adulthood.
source: The differences in lifestyle-related factors were maintained into young adulthood.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on longitudinal data.

claim: Most of the variation in biological aging shared with adolescent lifestyle was explained by common genetic factors.
source: Most of the variation in biological aging shared with adolescent lifestyle was explained by common genetic factors.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on quantitative genetic modeling.

claim: An unhealthy lifestyle during pubertal years is associated with accelerated biological aging in young adulthood.
source: These findings suggest that an unhealthy lifestyle during pubertal years is associated with accelerated biological aging in young adulthood.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: Genetic pleiotropy may largely explain the observed associations between adolescent lifestyle and biological aging.
source: Genetic pleiotropy may largely explain the observed associations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study findings based on genetic modeling results.

claim: A total of 5600 twins and their families initially enrolled in the FinnTwin12 study.
source: A total of 5600 twins and their families initially enrolled in the study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: The response rates were high for each assessment (85–90%).
source: The response rates were high for each assessment (85–90%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study response rates.

claim: A total of 1295 twins of the FinnTwin12 cohort were examined and measured either in-person or through telephonic interviews.
source: A total of 1295 twins of the FinnTwin12 cohort were examined and measured either in-person or through telephonic interviews.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: DNAm was determined and biological aging was assessed for 847 twins, out of which 824 twins had also information on lifestyle-related habits in adolescence.
source: DNAm was determined and biological aging was assessed for 847 twins, out of which 824 twins had also information on lifestyle-related habits in adolescence.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: Of the samples included in this study, 744 were assayed using 450k and 80 samples using EPIC arrays.
source: Of the samples included in this study, 744 were assayed using 450k and 80 samples using EPIC arrays.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methods.

claim: The mean age (SD) of the twins having information on biological aging was 22.4 (0.7) years.
source: The mean age (SD) of the twins having information on biological aging was 22.4 (0.7) years.
evidence: This is a direct statement of descriptive statistics from the study.

claim: The means of the epigenetic age estimates were estimated as follows: Horvath's clock 28.9 (3.6), Hannum's clock 18.2 (3.3), DNAm PhenoAge 13.0 (5.3), and DNAm GrimAge 25.2 (3.3) years.
source: The means of the epigenetic age estimates were estimated as follows: Horvath's clock 28.9 (3.6), Hannum's clock 18.2 (3.3), DNAm PhenoAge 13.0 (5.3), and DNAm GrimAge 25.2 (3.3) years.
evidence: This is a direct statement of descriptive statistics from the study.

claim: The intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) of epigenetic aging measures were consistently higher in MZ twin pairs than in DZ twin pairs.
source: The intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) of epigenetic aging measures were consistently higher in MZ twin pairs than in DZ twin pairs (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on data presented in Table 2.

claim: Higher ICCs in MZ twin pairs than in DZ twin pairs suggests an underlying genetic component in biological aging.
source: This suggests an underlying genetic component in biological aging.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ICC data based on twin study methodology.

claim: The correlations between the different epigenetic aging measures ranged from –0.12 to 0.73.
source: The correlations between the different epigenetic aging measures ranged from –0.12 to 0.73.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on correlation analysis.

claim: The lowest correlation was observed between AAHorvath and DunedinPoAm and between AAHorvath and DunedinPACE.
source: The lowest correlation was observed between AAHorvath and DunedinPoAm and between AAHorvath and DunedinPACE.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on correlation analysis.

claim: The highest correlations (>0.5) were observed between AAHannum and AAPheno, AAGrim and DunedinPoAm, and DunedinPoAm and DunedinPACE.
source: The highest correlations (>0.5) were observed between AAHannum and AAPheno, AAGrim and DunedinPoAm, and DunedinPoAm and DunedinPACE.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on correlation analysis.

claim: Of the participants, 32% fell into the class of healthiest lifestyle habits (C1).
source: Of the participants, 32% fell into the class of healthiest lifestyle habits (C1) (see Figure 2, and the distributions of indicator variables according to the adolescent lifestyle behavior patterns in Table 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on latent class analysis, with reference to Figure 2 and Table 4.

claim: Every fifth (19.9%) participant belonged to the second class (C2), characterized by the low mean level of BMI in the range of normal weight for children (low-normal BMI).
source: Every fifth (19.9%) participant belonged to the second class (C2), characterized by the low mean level of BMI in the range of normal weight for children (low-normal BMI) (Cole et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on latent class analysis, with reference to Cole et al., 2007 for BMI classification.

claim: The participants placed in the third class (C3, 22.8%) had lifestyle habits similar to those of the participants in class C1; however, they had a higher level of BMI in the range of normal weight for children (high-normal BMI).
source: The participants placed in the third class (C3, 22.8%) had lifestyle habits similar to those of the participants in class C1; however, they had a higher level of BMI in the range of normal weight for children (high-normal BMI).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on latent class analysis.

claim: About every tenth (9.5%) of the participants belonged to the fourth class (C4), with the highest level of BMI (high BMI).
source: About every tenth (9.5%) of the participants belonged to the fourth class (C4), with the highest level of BMI (high BMI).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on latent class analysis.

claim: At each measurement point, the mean BMI level of class C4 exceeded the cutoff points for overweight in children.
source: At each measurement point, the mean BMI level exceeded the cutoff points for overweight in children (Cole et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding with reference to Cole et al., 2007 for BMI classification.

claim: Of the participants, 15.9% were classified into the subgroup characterized by the unhealthiest lifestyle behaviors (C5).
source: Of the participants, 15.9% were classified into the subgroup characterized by the unhealthiest lifestyle behaviors (C5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on latent class analysis.

claim: Most participants in class C5 were daily smokers and used alcohol regularly at the age of 17.
source: Most of them were daily smokers and used alcohol regularly at the age of 17.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding describing class C5.

claim: Boys were slightly over-represented in the classes that were most physically active (C1, C3) and had the highest levels of BMI (C3, C4).
source: Boys were slightly over-represented in the classes that were most physically active (C1, C3) and had the highest levels of BMI (C3, C4) (percentage of boys: C1: 57.2%; C3: 51.5%; and C4: 52.7%), and under-represented in the classes with lowest levels of BMI (C2) and the unhealthiest lifestyle behavior pattern (C5) (C2: 42.7%; C5: 44.1%).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on descriptive statistics.

claim: There were differences in pubertal development at baseline between the groups.
source: There were also differences in pubertal development at baseline between the groups.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on descriptive statistics.

claim: The subgroups with the highest levels of BMI (C3, C4) and the class with unhealthiest lifestyle habits (C5) were, on average, the most advanced in pubertal development.
source: The subgroups with the highest levels of BMI (C3, C4) and the class with unhealthiest lifestyle habits (C5) were, on average, the most advanced in pubertal development (mean PDS, C3: 1.67 95% CI: [1.63–1.71], C4: 1.69 [1.64–1.74]; and C5: 1.68 [1.63–1.72]), while the class with the healthiest lifestyle pattern (C1) and that with the lowest level of BMI (C2) were less advanced in pubertal development (C1: 1.53 [1.50–1.56]; C2: 1.44 [1.41–1.47]).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on descriptive statistics.

claim: In the subsample, the differences in lifestyle-related factors were maintained well over the transition from adolescence to young adulthood.
source: In the subsample, the differences in lifestyle-related factors were maintained well over the transition from adolescence to young adulthood (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were differences among the classes in AAPheno (Wald test: p=0.006), AAGrim (p=2.3e-11), DunedinPoAm (p=3.1e-9), and DunedinPACE (p=5.5e-7) in the models adjusted for sex, age, and baseline pubertal development.
source: There were differences among the classes in AAPheno (Wald test: p=0.006), AAGrim (p=2.3e-11), DunedinPoAm (p=3.1e-9), and DunedinPACE (p=5.5e-7) in the models adjusted for sex, age, and baseline pubertal development.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on statistical analysis.

claim: There were no differences in biological aging when Horvath's clock (p=0.550) and Hannum's clock (p=0.487) were used.
source: There were no differences in biological aging when Horvath's clock (p=0.550) and Hannum's clock (p=0.487) were used.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on statistical analysis.

claim: The group with the unhealthiest lifestyle pattern (C5) was, on average, 1.7–3.3 years biologically older than the groups with healthier lifestyle patterns and normal weight (C1–C3) when DNAm GrimAge was used to assess biological aging.
source: The group with the unhealthiest lifestyle pattern (C5) was, on average, 1.7–3.3 years biologically older than the groups with healthier lifestyle patterns and normal weight (C1–C3) when DNAm GrimAge was used to assess biological aging (Table 5, M1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding with reference to Table 5.

claim: The unhealthiest group had, on average, 2–3 weeks/calendar year faster pace of biological aging, as measured with DunedinPoAm.
source: Moreover, the unhealthiest group had, an average, 2–3 weeks/calendar year faster pace of biological aging, as measured with DunedinPoAm.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on statistical analysis.

claim: When DNAm GrimAge was used, the group with a high BMI (C4) was, on average, 1.8–2.4 years biologically older than the two groups with healthier lifestyle patterns (C1 and C2).
source: When DNAm GrimAge was used, the group with a high BMI (C4) was, on average, 1.8–2.4 years biologically older than the two groups with healthier lifestyle patterns (C1 and C2) (Table 5, M1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding with reference to Table 5.

claim: When measured with the DunedinPoAm estimator, the class C4 had, on average, 3–4 weeks/calendar year faster pace of aging.
source: When measured with the DunedinPoAm estimator, the class had, on average, 3–4 weeks/calendar year faster pace of aging, and when measured with the DunedinPACE estimator, it had 4–5 weeks/calendar year faster pace of aging.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on statistical analysis.

claim: When measured with the DunedinPACE estimator, class C4 had 4–5 weeks/calendar year faster pace of aging.
source: When measured with the DunedinPoAm estimator, the class had, on average, 3–4 weeks/calendar year faster pace of aging, and when measured with the DunedinPACE estimator, it had 4–5 weeks/calendar year faster pace of aging.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on statistical analysis.

claim: When DNAm PhenoAge was used to assess biological aging, only the group with a high BMI stood out.
source: When DNAm PhenoAge was used to assess biological aging, only the group with a high BMI stood out.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on statistical analysis.

claim: The group with high BMI was biologically 2.0–2.5 years older than the groups with lower mean levels of BMI (C1–C2, C5) when DNAm PhenoAge was used.
source: The group was biologically 2.0–2.5 years older than the groups with lower mean levels of BMI (C1–C2, C5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on statistical analysis.

claim: Baseline pubertal development was associated with advanced biological aging only when Hannum's clock was used to derive biological AA.
source: Based on the estimation results of the models, baseline pubertal development was associated with advanced biological aging only when Hannum's clock was used to derive biological AA (standardized regression coefficient B = 0.10 [0.01–0.18]).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on statistical analysis.

claim: After additionally adjusting the model for BMI in adulthood, the differences in AAPheno and DunedinPACE between the class of participants with high BMI (C4) and those with lower BMI (C1, C2, C5) were attenuated.
source: After additionally adjusting the model for BMI in adulthood, the differences in AAPheno and DunedinPACE between the class of participants with high BMI (C4) and those with lower BMI (C1, C2, C5) were attenuated (Table 5, M2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding with reference to Table 5.

claim: The observed differences in biological aging between high BMI and lower BMI classes are probably fully mediated by BMI in adulthood when AAPheno and DunedinPACE are used.
source: This finding suggests that the observed differences in biological aging probably are fully mediated by BMI in adulthood.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the attenuation of differences after adjusting for adult BMI.

claim: The differences in biological aging were only slightly attenuated when the DNAm GrimAge and DunedinPoAm estimators were used after adjusting for adult BMI.
source: However, the differences in biological aging were only slightly attenuated when the DNAm GrimAge and DunedinPoAm estimators were used, suggesting that childhood overweight may leave permanent imprint on biological aging assessed with these measures.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on statistical analysis.

claim: Childhood overweight may leave permanent imprint on biological aging assessed with DNAm GrimAge and DunedinPoAm.
source: However, the differences in biological aging were only slightly attenuated when the DNAm GrimAge and DunedinPoAm estimators were used, suggesting that childhood overweight may leave permanent imprint on biological aging assessed with these measures.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the persistence of differences after adjusting for adult BMI.

claim: There were differences in DNAm-based ADM (Wald test: p=0.010), B2M (p=0.014), and Packyrs (p=1.3e-5) between the adolescent lifestyle behavior patterns after controlling for sex, age, and baseline pubertal development.
source: Overall, after controlling for sex, age, and baseline pubertal development, there were differences in DNAm-based ADM (Wald test: p=0.010), B2M (p=0.014), and Packyrs (p=1.3e-5), but not in DNAm-based cystatin C (p=0.140), GDF15 (p=0.228), Leptin (p=0.228), PAI-1 (p=0.055), and TIMP-1 (p=0.089) between the adolescent lifestyle behavior patterns.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on statistical analysis.

claim: There were no differences in DNAm-based cystatin C (p=0.140), GDF15 (p=0.228), Leptin (p=0.228), PAI-1 (p=0.055), and TIMP-1 (p=0.089) between the adolescent lifestyle behavior patterns.
source: Overall, after controlling for sex, age, and baseline pubertal development, there were differences in DNAm-based ADM (Wald test: p=0.010), B2M (p=0.014), and Packyrs (p=1.3e-5), but not in DNAm-based cystatin C (p=0.140), GDF15 (p=0.228), Leptin (p=0.228), PAI-1 (p=0.055), and TIMP-1 (p=0.089) between the adolescent lifestyle behavior patterns.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on statistical analysis.

claim: The class with the unhealthiest lifestyle habits (C5) differed unfavorably from the other classes only by DNAm smoking pack-years.
source: The class with the unhealthiest lifestyle habits (C5) differed unfavorably from the other classes only by DNAm smoking pack-years while the class of participants with high BMI (C4) stood out by several DNAm-based plasma proteins including DNAm ADM, PAI-1, and TIMP-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The class of participants with high BMI (C4) stood out by several DNAm-based plasma proteins including DNAm ADM, PAI-1, and TIMP-1.
source: The class with the unhealthiest lifestyle habits (C5) differed unfavorably from the other classes only by DNAm smoking pack-years while the class of participants with high BMI (C4) stood out by several DNAm-based plasma proteins including DNAm ADM, PAI-1, and TIMP-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model including additive genetic and non-shared environmental component (AE model) was considered optimal for all the epigenetic aging measures.
source: The model including additive genetic and non-shared environmental component (AE model) was considered optimal for all the epigenetic aging measures (Table 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on model fitting with reference to Table 6.

claim: Genetic factors explained 62–73% of the total variation in biological aging depending on the estimator.
source: Genetic factors explained 62–73% of the total variation in biological aging depending on the estimator.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on quantitative genetic modeling.

claim: Unshared environmental factors explained 27–38% of the total variation in biological aging.
source: The rest of the variation (27–38%) was explained by unshared environmental factors.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on quantitative genetic modeling.

claim: The proportion of the total variation in biological aging in early adulthood explained by adolescent lifestyle behavior patterns was 3.7% for AAPheno, 16.8% for AAGrim, 15.4% for DunedinPoAm, and 10.5% for DunedinPACE.
source: The proportion of the total variation in biological aging in early adulthood explained by adolescent lifestyle behavior patterns was 3.7% for AAPheno, 16.8% for AAGrim, 15.4% for DunedinPoAm, and 10.5% for DunedinPACE (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The association between adolescent lifestyle patterns and biological aging in early adulthood was largely explained by shared genetic influences.
source: The association between adolescent lifestyle patterns and biological aging in early adulthood was largely explained by shared genetic influences; the genetic factors shared with adolescent lifestyle explained 3.7, 13.1, 12.6, and 10.5%, respectively, of the total variation in biological aging.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on quantitative genetic modeling.

claim: Depending on the biological aging estimate, only 0–3.7% of the total variation in biological aging was explained by (unshared) environmental factors shared with adolescent lifestyle patterns.
source: Depending on the biological aging estimate, only 0–3.7% of the total variation in biological aging was explained by (unshared) environmental factors shared with adolescent lifestyle patterns.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding based on quantitative genetic modeling.

claim: Most participants generally followed healthy lifestyle patterns.
source: In our study, most participants generally followed healthy lifestyle patterns, but we could also identify a group of young adults characterized by higher BMI (10% of all participants) in adolescence, as well as a group (16% of all participants) with more frequent co-occurrence of smoking, binge drinking, and low levels of physical activity in adolescence.

claim: The distribution of the lifestyle-related patterns in the subsample of twins with information on biological aging was similar to the distribution in large cohort data, supporting the generalizability of the findings.
source: Moreover, adolescent lifestyle behavior patterns were identified using data-driven LCA. This approach enabled us to use all available data on adolescent lifestyle-related behaviors and identify the patterns without using artificial cutoff points for the variables. The reciprocal associations between different lifestyle-related factors, as well as their joint association with biological aging, are complex, and individual associations are difficult to interpret. However, our approach produced results with easy interpretation. The data were prospective, and biological aging was assessed with novel epigenetic aging measures, including a recently published DunedinPACE estimator.
evidence: This is a statement about the generalizability of the findings based on the similarity of distributions.
